title: Review: Yes, we're still arguing about Nolan's The Odyssey
gist: Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey has cleared $700 million against a $250 million budget — beating Oppenheimer's entire haul — while remaining a culture-war lightning rod, culminating in classicist Emily Wilson's hostile London Review of Books essay. The reviewer defends the film as a memory-driven contemporary remix in which limited screen time for a star cast is a deliberate structural choice, and argues Wilson judged the film against Homer rather than against Nolan's stated artistic intent.

themes.theme: Box office scale and inevitable backlash

insights.claim: Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey has topped $700 million at the box office against a $250 million production budget, surpassing the entire haul of his previous film Oppenheimer.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Confirms that a nearly three-hour auteur adaptation of an ancient poem can clear blockbuster economics, strengthening the case for premium-format original-IP theatrical bets.
insights.locator: The Odyssey has garnered both critical and audience raves

insights.claim: The film is expected to draw many Oscar nominations and several wins across both technical achievement and performance categories, with Samantha Morton, Matt Damon, Anne Hathaway, Tom Holland and Robert Pattinson singled out.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Awards runway extends the theatrical and home-release tail of a title that has already recouped its budget nearly three times over.
insights.locator: It’s going to be nominated for tons of Oscars

insights.claim: A manufactured online trolling and culture-war campaign preceding release had no discernible effect on the film's commercial performance, and its very success then triggered a second wave of backlash.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Pre-release online outrage is a poor predictor of box office — a useful discount to apply when social sentiment is used to forecast opening weekends.
insights.locator: The manufactured online trolling/culture war campaign

insights.claim: The film opens with a bard, played by Travis Scott, telling the idealized heroic version of Troy's fall that his audiences want to hear, framing the entire story as mediated myth rather than direct depiction.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: The framing device is the key to reading the film's omissions as intentional rather than as failures of adaptation.
insights.locator: Nolan sets the tone by opening with a bard

insights.claim: Nolan preserves Homer's nonlinear tales-within-tales structure and presents Odysseus as a broken man recovering fractured memories of the Trojan War after years under the effects of lotus fruit with Calypso on Ogygia.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Memory-recovery structure is the same device Nolan has used across his filmography — evidence that this is a Nolan film in Homeric clothing, not an adaptation exercise.
insights.locator: The director has also preserved Homer’s nonlinear narrative structure

insights.claim: The film's central revelation is Odysseus admitting to Penelope that his prolonged absence was driven partly by a stricken conscience over the horror his own cleverness unleashed on Troy.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Recasting the hero's wandering as avoidance of guilt rather than divine obstruction is the film's actual argument — and what distinguishes it from prior screen versions.
insights.locator: It all builds up to a powerful moment of self-revelation with Penelope

insights.claim: Nolan deliberately reduced the role of the gods, aiming to humanize them and convey supernatural events through natural phenomena that ancient audiences would have read as divine influence.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: A stated directorial intent that reframes the most common critique of the film as a disagreement about goals rather than a defect in execution.
insights.locator: She’s unhappy that the gods don’t play a larger role

insights.claim: Major stars including Charlize Theron, Lupita Nyong'o in a dual role, Jon Bernthal and Benny Safdie get only minutes of screen time because Nolan presumes audience familiarity with Homer and keeps these figures in the margins of Odysseus' memory.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Casting expensive stars in near-cameos is a distribution and marketing strategy as much as a creative one — and a predictable source of critical complaint.
insights.quote: But minutes of screen time are not necessarily indicative of the relative importance of any given role to Nolan’s vision.
insights.locator: This approach gives the audience a sense of what Odysseus is experiencing

insights.claim: Zendaya's Athena appears only in brief dream-like sequences yet carries the film's moral arc, shifting from neutrality to horrified grief when Greek soldiers behead her temple statue alongside a Trojan woman bearing her face.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Demonstrates the review's core defense — narrative weight is carried by compressed symbolic scenes, so screen-time-based criticism misreads the design.
insights.locator: For instance, Zendaya’s Athena only appears

insights.claim: Elliot Page plays Sinon, a character absent from Homer's Odyssey and drawn from Virgil's Aeneid, retooled by Nolan into an innocent victim who dies for a scheme he did not understand and returns as an accusatory shadow in the underworld.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Importing and rewriting a non-Homeric character is concrete evidence the film is a remix rather than a translation — the point on which the whole critical fight turns.
insights.locator: Similarly, Elliot Page is only in a couple of small scenes as Sinon

insights.claim: Samantha Morton's Circe is reinvented from Homer's seductress into a woman who has suffered at the hands of men and transforms Odysseus' crew into pigs because she sees them as swine in human masks, delivering the most powerful sequence in the film.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: The most-praised performance comes from the most heavily rewritten character, which argues against fidelity as the standard for adaptation quality.
insights.quote: she turns Odysseus’ men into pigs because to her, they are swine wearing human masks
insights.locator: Nobody makes more of their limited screentime than Samantha Morton

insights.claim: Classicist Emily Wilson, translator of Homer's epic, published a harsh critique of the film in the London Review of Books after Nolan repeatedly quoted her translation's opening line, "Tell me about a complicated man," in interviews.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Shows how a director's own citation of a scholar can manufacture the highest-profile negative review of his film — a self-inflicted publicity dynamic.
insights.quote: Tell me about a complicated man

insights.claim: Wilson's specific objections are that the film centers Odysseus' point of view, that race-neutral casting leaves non-white actors playing variations on the "Black best friend" (a line she later walked back on BlueSky), that its implicit values diverge from Homer's, that it never explicitly shows war is bad or gives the victims of Troy a perspective, that it lacks sex scenes, sidelines female roles, and minimizes the gods.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: A catalogue of the actual academic objections, useful for separating substantive craft criticism from disagreement over what the adaptation should have been.

insights.claim: Wilson claimed to assess the film on its merits and the director's artistic intent yet never engages Nolan's stated intent regarding the gods, and her objection to filming in occupied Western Sahara — potentially valid on its own terms — is unrelated to evaluating the film itself.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Identifies the reviewable failure mode of expert criticism: judging a work against the critic's preferred version rather than the creator's stated project.
insights.quote: I would be ashamed to have written any part of this script.
insights.locator: There’s more. Wilson hates the dialogue.

insights.claim: Wilson's dismissal is self-undermining, since a film she describes as simplistic, shallow and fleetingly forgettable would not sustain the passionate argument her own lengthy essay extends.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Cultural durability is measured by sustained argument, not review scores — a heuristic for spotting franchise-capable properties.
insights.quote: If Nolan’s Odyssey is so simplistic and shallow and fleetingly forgettable as Wilson claims, why are we still arguing so passionately about it?
insights.locator: If Nolan’s Odyssey is so simplistic and shallow

insights.claim: Every adaptation is a translation carrying its own tradeoffs and the translator's personal stamp — Wilson's own version uses iambic pentameter instead of Greek dactylic hexameter — so no single authoritative rendering of Homer's Odyssey exists.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: A reusable standard for judging adaptations of public-domain source material: evaluate the tradeoffs chosen, not the distance from the original.
insights.quote: There is no such thing as the One True Take on Homer’s Odyssey.
insights.locator: Ultimately that’s what every translator does

insights.claim: Clunky dialogue is not disqualifying for a film's cultural standing, as demonstrated by Star Wars: A New Hope becoming a cultural touchstone despite the same flaw.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Craft defects weigh far less than mythic resonance in determining a film's long-run cultural and commercial value.
insights.quote: if bad dialogue were enough to sink a film, Star Wars: A New Hope would have bombed at the box office
insights.locator: Is the dialogue a bit clunky?

insights.claim: The reviewer's verdict is that Nolan succeeded brilliantly at a contemporary remix filtered through his personal themes while falling shy of masterpiece status, and that the audience split ultimately tracks whether a viewer already likes Nolan's directorial style.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Auteur brand, not source material, is the real segmentation variable for this film's audience — the same dynamic that will drive its home-release and rewatch demand.
insights.quote: usual combination of grandiosity and superficiality
